main.t: A single, complex bone in the centre of the skull base that joins almost every other skull bone (sphenoid bone).

simpler.t: The sphenoid is a winged bone in the middle of the floor of the skull.

deeper.t: It is one of the eight bones of the brain case.

facts.t: It forms much of the floor of the middle of the skull base.
Its outer parts reach the sides of the skull, just in front of the temporal bone.
Behind each eye, it forms the back wall of the eye socket (orbit).

simpler.t: The sphenoid sits deep in the middle of your head, behind your eyes.

deeper.t: Because it joins with almost every other bone of the skull, it is called a “keystone” bone.

items.name: Lesser wings
items.t: Form the ridge between the front and middle hollows (fossae) of the skull floor.

items.name: Greater wings
items.t: Form the front of the middle fossa and part of the side of the skull.

items.name: Sella turcica
items.t: A saddle-shaped seat in the midline. Its hollow (hypophyseal fossa) holds the pituitary gland.

items.name: Optic canal
items.t: Beside the sella turcica. It carries the optic nerve from the eye to the brain.

items.name: Superior orbital fissure
items.t: A slit into the back of the orbit. It carries nerves to the eye muscles and the forehead.

items.name: Foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
items.t: Openings in the floor of the middle fossa for nerves to the face and an artery to the brain’s coverings.
items.check: OpenStax places these in the floor of the middle cranial fossa; that they lie in the sphenoid’s greater wing is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

items.name: Medial and lateral pterygoid plates
items.t: Thin wing-shaped plates underneath. The lateral plates anchor chewing muscles.

items.name: Sphenoid sinus
items.t: An air-filled space in its body: the most posterior paranasal sinus.

simpler.t: It has wings, a saddle that holds the pituitary gland and holes for nerves to the eye and face.

deeper.t: Its lesser wings mark the border between the front (anterior) and middle cranial fossae.

facts.t: Its central position lets it act as a keystone, linking almost every other bone of the skull.
Nerves and vessels pass through its openings between the brain and the eye, face and jaws.
Its air-filled sinus lightens the skull and adds resonance to the voice.

simpler.t: It locks the skull bones together and lets nerves pass through to the face.

items.name: Pituitary gland
items.t: Sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica.

items.name: Nerves to the eye muscles
items.t: Pass through the superior orbital fissure.

items.name: Maxillary nerve
items.t: Leaves through the foramen rotundum to supply the cheek, nose and upper teeth.
items.check: OpenStax describes the nerve without naming it; “maxillary nerve” needs an approved source.

items.name: Middle meningeal artery
items.t: Enters through the foramen spinosum to supply the coverings of the brain.
items.check: OpenStax describes the artery without naming it; “middle meningeal artery” needs an approved source.

items.name: Chewing muscles
items.t: Attach to the lateral pterygoid plates.

items.name: Pterion
items.t: Its greater wing is one of four bones meeting at the pterion, the thinnest part of the skull.

simpler.t: The pituitary gland sits on it, and nerves to the eye and face pass through it.

facts.t: Bones of the skull base form by replacing cartilage with bone (endochondral ossification).
The size of the sphenoid sinus varies a great deal from person to person.

items.injury: A tumour of the pituitary gland grows upwards out of the sella turcica.
items.damaged: The optic chiasm, where nerve fibres from the two eyes cross.
items.cannotDo: See objects to the right and left: the outer parts of both visual fields are lost.
items.why: The crossing fibres sit just above the pituitary gland and are pressed on first.

items.injury: A hard blow to the side of the head at the pterion.
items.damaged: The artery just inside the skull there; blood collects and presses on the brain.
items.cannotDo: Stay well: the patient may seem fine at first, then worsen and can die within hours without treatment.
items.why: The pterion is the thinnest part of the skull, with a major artery right under it.

items.q: Explain why the sphenoid is called the keystone of the skull.
model: It is a single bone in the centre of the skull base.
Almost every other bone of the skull joins with it.
It forms much of the central skull base and part of the sides.
Parts of the cranial fossae and the back of each orbit are sphenoid bone.

items.q: A pituitary tumour grows up out of the sella turcica. Predict the visual problem and explain it.
model: It presses on the optic chiasm just above.
The crossing fibres are affected; fibres to the same side are not.
The outer part of the visual field is lost on both sides.
The patient cannot see objects to their left and right.

items.q: Compare the optic canal and the superior orbital fissure.
model: Optic canal: at the front outer corner of the sella turcica.
Superior orbital fissure: beside the optic canal, under the lesser wing.
It carries nerves to the eye muscles and sensory nerves to the forehead.

check.stem: What sits in the sella turcica?
check.why: The hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica holds the pituitary gland.

check.stem: Which opening carries the optic nerve?
check.why: The optic canal, beside the sella turcica, carries the optic nerve.

check.stem: What attaches to the lateral pterygoid plates?
check.why: The lateral pterygoid plates anchor chewing muscles that act on the mandible.
